Plain answers about Teme: what it is, where it stands, what it needs and what it does not do.

A content management system for publications: newsrooms, magazines and blogs with long archives. You write, publish and run the site from one admin, on your own server. It is built on Laravel and PostgreSQL.
Not yet. Teme is in alpha, at 0.7.0-alpha.1, and runs only on test sites. Version 1.0 is the first release meant for anyone to install. Follow the build on GitHub to see each release.
Can I try it without installing?
Not yet. A playground, a site you can open and try in the browser, is planned for later.
Yes. Teme is open source under the MIT licence: the core, the contracts package and the default theme. You may use it for any site, commercial or not.
Plugins and themes may carry their own licences, and some may be paid.
Teme is open source under the MIT licence, made by Krafty Sprouts Media, LLC.
Can one install run several sites?
No. One install runs one site. To run several sites, install Teme for each.
Can I sell things with it?
Teme has no shop or checkout. It is made for publishing.
No freeform visual page builder. Articles are written in the editor with cards for pictures, quotes, callouts and more; the theme sets the layout, with regions an administrator fills.
Will it run on shared hosting?
No. Teme needs a server you control, with Docker. Dokploy and Coolify make that simple, and a plain VPS works too.
Will my WordPress plugins and themes work?
No, they do not run on Teme. The importer brings your content, people and addresses across; features come from Teme itself or from Teme plugins.
Can I move my site to a new domain later?
Yes. Links and pictures are stored by what they point to, not by address, so a new domain is one change in configuration.
How is my content kept safe?
Backups run every night, encrypted with a recovery key you keep, and each is checked. The whole site can also be exported as JSON files.
Teme has a read-only API, off until you turn it on, for sites and apps that read your content. Writing through an API is not built.
The foundation is built: every item has a language, and translations are linked. The screens to manage languages come in a later release.
Questions and problems: open an issue on

pages.title: How a plugin could reach the directory.
pages.excerpt: Five steps from a package to every Teme site that wants it: built, submitted, checked, reviewed by a person, then signed and listed. Nothing here is built or decided.

attrs.alt: A diagram of the proposal: the author’s package goes to automatic checks, then to a review where an AI writes a report and a person decides, then into the signed index that Teme sites read.

content.text: The author builds the plugin as a package, with its manifest (what it asks permission for) and its icon.
The author submits the repository’s address.

The manifest is valid; it declares every capability it uses; it never writes code at run time; its dependencies have no known vulnerabilities; its licence is stated; it installs, and its tests pass, on the current Teme.
An AI reviewer reads the code against Teme’s rules and writes a report of its concerns. A person on the Teme team decides: approve, ask for changes, or refuse with reasons.
Each release is signed and added to the directory’s signed index, which every Teme site reads for installs and updates. A listed release never changes; a fix is a new version.
A release stays out of the directory until its review is done. A version that asks for more than the last one says so on its page, and each site asks its administrator again before it runs.
Whether an AI may ever approve alone.
What happens when a published plugin is found unsafe: it is pulled from the index and sites are told, but how, and how fast, is open.

docs.title: Proxies and HTTPS
docs.excerpt: Teme never serves HTTPS itself. A proxy in front of it, yours or your platform's, ends HTTPS and passes requests on. This page explains how Teme learns a reader's real address and whether the request was secure, which settings control that, and how to check it.

fields.written_for: the edge settings Teme reads at its own tag

content.text: Teme never serves HTTPS itself. A proxy in front of it, yours or your platform's, ends HTTPS and passes requests on. This page explains how Teme learns a reader's real address and whether the request was secure, which settings control that, and how to check it.
How a reader's address reaches Teme
A request passes through several hops:
Your proxy: Traefik, in Dokploy, Coolify and the plain-VPS recipe.
Each proxy adds the address it received the request from to a header called
, and says whether the reader used HTTPS in
. Teme believes those headers only from the proxies you list in
. From anyone else it ignores them, because anyone can send a header. If Teme trusted every sender, one reader could invent any address and walk past every limit that counts requests by address.
nginx never takes the address from a header. The image’s CI checks that.
A comma-separated list of addresses and ranges, plus two names:
means the three ranges that Docker networks use:
When you leave it unset, production trusts
and nothing else, and every other environment trusts no proxy. When you set it, even to nothing, it means exactly what you wrote. Teme refuses to start if it contains
or a range that covers every address, because trusting everything is the mistake that setting exists to prevent.
For one proxy on the Docker network, which is the recipe’s layout, you set nothing. Behind Cloudflare and Traefik, set
, and make Traefik trust Cloudflare as well;

attrs.alt: Teme Default's front page on a wide screen, in an invented newsroom: a lead story with its picture, a row of pinned stories and a feed of stories below.
Teme Default's front page on a phone: the header with its menu button, the lead story and the first stories of the feed in a single column.

content.text: Drawn from the theme's own colours and type, light and dark following the reader. The newsroom is invented.
Two menus, Header and Footer; on small screens the header menu opens without JavaScript. One region after the article, for up to five callout or button cards.
Header layout, colour scheme, the lead story, list or grid, featured images, author box, related posts and more, previewed on Settings › Design before they are published.
One heading per page, labelled menus, visible focus, and rules for reduced motion and forced colours, checked by tests on every template.
Its templates: latest posts, articles, pages (default and full width), archives, search, comments and not found. Nothing needs JavaScript to read.
